doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Learning xylophone and performing as a child
summary: Skipped grades, he started on xylophone because he was too young for trumpet; he and his sister performed in church shows.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I want to come back to that, “Rock Around the Clock” in a bit. But you started out on like xylophone or a mallet type instrument?

Yeah. Basically I was already young for my year in school. I started school I think I was four and a half, and the teachers, one of the teachers said, after first grade said, “You really don’t have to stay in second grade.” I was pretty smart. And since I was already young for the age, another teacher came to my folks and said, “Instead of skipping him into third grade, why don’t we give him some outside interest to take up his time and things.” And I couldn’t — I was too young to play the trumpet, my father played the trumpet, because my second set of front teeth weren’t firm and we were not rich enough to buy a piano, so my father went out and bought a xylophone and I learned to play xylophone before piano. I still play vibes occasionally but not on a professional level. But I do think it was important also because I think it’s important that — it’s helpful for musicians to play an instrument where they can visualize the notes. I mean when you see a chord — people always ask what goes through your mind when you’re playing — not

much — but in a way I can almost picture those notes, having played visually. And so until my second set of front teeth came in and firmed up I played xylophone. My sister sang. She was four years old, I was seven years old, and we were appearing in church minstrel shows and benefits and oh all kinds of stuff — talent contests. So we got started early. I loved the applause right from the start.
So you were learning to accompany also, on the xylophone?

I guess in a way, yeah. If you can picture a four year old standing on a milk crate, because to get up to the level of the microphone singing “The Things We Did Last Summer,” I mean this is like 1944 or so, in a show, a four-year-old girl singing “The Things We Did Last Summer.”
Too bad we don’t have it on video.
But was it in your mind, in your father’s mind, that you were going to play the trumpet when you were old enough?
